The figure above shows the graph of a function $y=f(x)$ and its inverse $y=f^{-1}(x).$ The point $A$ has coordinates $(2, 0)$ and lies on $y=f(x).$
The point $B$ has coordinates $(0,2)$ and lies on $y=f^{-1}(x).$ If $f'(2)=-\dfrac{3}{2},$ what is $(f^{-1})'(0)?$
examples.worked_solution:
Since $B \,(0,2)$ lies on $f^{-1},$ we have $f^{-1}(0) = 2.$ We're also told that $f'(2)=-\dfrac{3}{2}.$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse function is

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(x))}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(0) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
